AI amplifies what the organization already is ( ) . With AI at the engineer alone, quality assurance piles up and the Customer gets far less. Incomplete requirements were always the most named pain ( ) , and they come back as rework; clear requirements, good orders, lower the pressure. 2 How Ideal, Realistic, then a scenario's tour. Ideal, then Realistic; each scenario's tour sets the dials and runs to the week that matters; a click on a work center opens its dashboard. 3 What Every work center has two dials. Efficiency is output, how much it puts out; effectiveness is outcome, how much of it is good. AI raises the first and leaves the second alone. Specifying was always the hard part ( ) , and every work center is people and tools ( ) .

Play Pressure travels along the connections A change at one work center, such as faster code writing, reaches its neighbours: more code to review, build, test and release. The talk offers this as a scenario, not a measurement 1 (SWE-0001). Sources (1) Adam Bender, Software Engineering at the Tipping Point (conference talk, transcript) ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com Review is where the load lands On teams with high AI adoption, pull requests merged rose 98% while review time rose 91% and pull request size 154%, with no significant company-level gain. Vendor telemetry and an association, not a trial 1 (AIE-0018). Sources (1) Faros AI, The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025 (23 July 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) faros.ai Review can be skipped In a writing experiment 68% of professionals given a chatbot submitted its first output unedited. It was a short online task, so it may not hold for work someone is accountable for 1 (AIE-0019). Sources (1) Noy and Zhang, Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence ( opens in a new tab ) economics.mit.edu Product managers keep the accountability They hesitate to delegate specifications and say they are still accountable for AI-written output, so their effort moves to checking it. One company, self-reported 1 (AIE-0019). Sources (1) Ulloa et al., Product Manager Practices for Delegating Work to Generative AI: “Accountability must not be delegated to non-human actors” ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Muddy instructions cost accuracy Instructions that arrive incomplete over several turns lowered accuracy by 39% on average across tested models. That a clear requirement lowers this is an inference; no source tests it as an intervention 1 (LLM-0022). Sources (1) Laban et al., LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Sales and billing cards are inference Reps spend 30% of a week selling, from a vendor survey, which says nothing about review work growing. No source measures AI's effect on billing; the sales and billing card text is the general pattern applied, not evidence 1 (AIE-0019, AIE-0020). Sources (1) Salesforce, State of Sales, 6th Edition ( opens in a new tab ) assets.ctfassets.net

Why, how and what AI amplifies what is there AI's primary role is as an amplifier of an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses, and the greatest returns come from the underlying organizational system rather than the tools 1 (AIE-0018). Sources (1) DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 (overview page) ( opens in a new tab ) dora.dev Incomplete requirements are the most named pain 48% of 228 companies named incomplete or hidden requirements their most frequent requirements problem, with rework after implementation among the reported effects. Self-reported survey; frequency is not cost 1 (SWE-0002). Sources (1) Méndez Fernández et al., Naming the Pain in Requirements Engineering: Contemporary Problems, Causes, and Effects in Practice ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Specifying is the hard part (inference) Deciding precisely what to build is the hardest single part of building software. That AI moves the saved effort into specifying is an inference from this and the review findings; no source measures specification effort rising 1 (AIE-0018, AIE-0020). Sources (1) Brooks, No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accident in Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) worrydream.com A work center is people and technology A socio-technical system is a system made of people and technology, and an organization's structure shapes what it builds. The definitions are the speaker's paraphrase 1 (SWE-0001). Sources (1) Adam Bender, Software Engineering at the Tipping Point (conference talk, transcript) ( opens in a new tab ) youtube.com

Play 0:00 – 0:31 You know this cartoon tire swing cartoon game of telephone no bad actors ten times faster You all know this cartoon. Ten panels, and in every one a different role hears something different, so the swing that comes out is nothing like the one the customer wanted. Nobody in it is a bad actor: it is a game of telephone, where an intent nobody voiced well gets translated at every handoff, which means the fault sits in the system. With AI, the wrong swing gets built ten times faster. 0:31 – 1:01 The factory runs live runs live Who does what In theory In practice factory AI on Customer This one runs live, so nothing here rests on my word. It starts on Who does what, every department with its panel of the cartoon, steps into the factory through In theory and In practice, and then AI goes on. Every document on the belts is a task, the requests come from the Customer on the left, and the releases go back to the Customer. Watch what the Customer gets. 1:01 – 1:19 Map your team your own team work center is a role belt is a handoff slowest review step inspection Look at the factory as if it were your own team, where every work center is a role and every belt is a handoff. Find the slowest review step, the inspection, because that is where the work will pile up first. 1:19 – 1:40 Check the inspection before the turbo AI on one work center inspection after it review step neighbours pressure Now switch AI on at one work center. It got faster, but the inspection after it did not, so ask whether that review step can handle more. Watch the neighbours as well as the work center. My picture is that the pressure does not stay where you put the AI. 1:40 – 2:07 Fix the orders first analyst's effectiveness unclear requirements bad work rework complaints write the requirement clearly Now drop the analyst's effectiveness. Unclear requirements turn into bad work, and AI carries that bad work to every work center after it, faster than before, until it comes back as rework and complaints. So write the requirement clearly enough that someone new could act on it. This is my hypothesis: that is the step that lowers the pressure instead of moving it. 2:07 – 2:36 What the Customer got Customer card releases satisfied recap early not a measurement The Customer card is where the releases come back: what they got, and how satisfied they are. In most teams one work center looks like that inspection. To recap: map the team, check the inspection before the turbo, write the requirement clearly. It is a way of looking and still early, not a measurement of your team. The Explorable is here whenever you want to run it again.

Why, how and what 0:00 – 0:12 Why you may leave it short version why how what If you played it, you already have the picture, so this is the short version. One slide covers why it matters, how to use it and what it shows. 0:12 – 0:39 Why: the problem is the system unclear requirements nobody to blame review neighbours specifying hypothesis Unclear requirements were always expensive, and nobody in the chain was to blame for that. AI speeds execution up, so the work piles up at review, and my picture is that it spreads to the neighbours. This next part is my hypothesis: the effort moves into specifying too, because that was always the hard part, and nobody has measured it yet. 0:39 – 0:48 Clear orders lower it clear requirements good orders feed it something worth moving Clear requirements are good orders for the factory. AI moves whatever you feed it, faster, so feed it something worth moving. 0:48 – 1:02 How: play it Ideal Realistic scenario guided tour dials dashboard It starts in Ideal, then Realistic, and every scenario has a guided tour that sets the dials and runs to the week that matters; a click on any work center opens its dashboard. 1:02 – 1:19 What: two dials everywhere efficiency effectiveness AI raises the first review pressure Every work center has efficiency, how much it puts out, and effectiveness, how much of it is good. AI raises the first and leaves the second alone. Review stays as fast as it was, so that is where the pressure builds. 1:19 – 1:32 Take it back to Monday map your team check the review step write the requirement process owner Map your team, check the review step before you speed anything up, and write the requirement for someone new. Whoever owns that process knows where the pressure lands first.
